opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the more striking things in the results, and I think there are a few things going on.

Part of it is that the question we asked is a bit more specific than "can it write quicksort." The task description was something like: write concise, efficient, human-readable Python code to implement simple algorithms like quicksort, where the system learns this from specifications and examples rather than just having seen lots of quicksort implementations. So you could argue about whether ChatGPT is doing the thing we described or something adjacent to it. It's plausibly drawing on huge numbers of existing implementations in its training data, and that's not quite the "learn to do it from a spec" framing.

But honestly, I don't think that fully explains it. My guess is a lot of respondents just weren't tracking exactly where the frontier was at the time they answered. The survey went out in late 2023, and capabilities were moving really fast. Even people who are experts in machine learning broadly aren't necessarily playing with the latest chatbots every day and checking off which milestones have quietly been passed. And when you're answering a long survey with a lot of these tasks, you're probably giving a fairly quick, intuitive guess rather than going and testing it.

There's also an interesting general pattern where people seem to put things a bit in the future by default. If you ask "when will AI be able to do X," there's a framing effect where it sounds like it hasn't happened yet, so people give some number of years out. We've seen framing effects elsewhere in the survey that are pretty large, like asking for the probability by a given year versus the year by which there's a given probability gives quite different answers.

So I'd take it as a useful caution about how to read these forecasts. They're informative about what researchers collectively believe, and that matters in its own right, but they're not a precise oracle. When you see a forecast like that for something that already seems doable, it's a signal that the aggregate opinion may lag reality in places, and maybe that people are generally underestimating how quickly some of these things are arriving.

r001.rationale: It frames the task as learning from specifications and examples rather than relying on having seen many existing quicksort implementations.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish aggregate probability estimates from the percentage of respondents predicting the milestone.

r003.rationale: It does not question whether quicksort success generalizes reliably across comparable algorithm tasks.

r004.rationale: It does not identify that the question leaves the required success frequency unspecified.

r005.rationale: It says asking when AI will do something can frame it as not yet achieved, leading respondents to give a future date.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that one is genuinely a bit embarrassing, and I think there are a few things going on. The first is just that forecasting is hard, and a lot of the people we survey aren't paying close attention to exactly which tasks have been done. They're researchers working on their own corner of machine learning, and they might not have sat down and tried to get ChatGPT to write quicksort. So some of it is plain error, where people are answering based on a slightly stale picture of where things are.

But I think a second part is about how we worded the question. We asked about things like "write Python code for algorithms like quicksort, given a specification in natural language," and we also asked about the overall notion of a task being "feasible," which we defined as something a top lab could do within a year if they wanted to, with cost not being a huge factor. When you phrase it that way, some people interpret it quite strictly: does it get it right every time, reliably, without a human checking it? And by that standard you could argue it's not quite there, or at least it wasn't obviously there when people answered. Other people interpret it loosely and would say, of course, it's done. So you get a spread, and the median lands somewhere that looks odd.

There's also the thing that quicksort specifically is a bad example, because it's in every textbook and every training corpus. It's almost a memorization task. If you asked about writing a novel algorithm from a spec, you'd get a very different answer, and I suspect some respondents were mentally substituting the harder version of the task when they answered.

And then the broader point I'd take from it is just a reminder about how to read these surveys. They're useful as a snapshot of what a large group of people who work in the field believe, and for seeing how those beliefs shift over time. In 2022 to 2023 they shifted a lot, with timelines coming in quite dramatically. But they're not a careful aggregation of expert judgment where everyone has done their homework on each item. So when one of the items looks obviously wrong, I think the right response is to lower your confidence in the specific numbers a bit, while still taking seriously the overall shape, which is that people in the field think quite transformative capabilities are coming, and much sooner than they thought a few years ago.

r001.rationale: It contrasts textbook quicksort, which is likely memorized from training data, with writing a novel algorithm from a specification.

r002.rationale: It discusses the survey median and respondent beliefs but does not distinguish aggregate probabilities from the percentage of respondents predicting the milestone.

r003.rationale: It says quicksort is a poor example and contrasts it with novel algorithms, while noting that respondents may expect reliable, unchecked success.

r004.rationale: It describes differing strict and loose interpretations of feasibility, but does not clearly identify that the question leaves the required success frequency unspecified.

r005.rationale: It does not suggest that the mere inclusion of a capability on the survey led respondents to infer that AI could not yet perform it.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a good reason to be cautious about interpreting these numbers. If a system can already do the task, then a forecast placing it in the future is clearly missing something—unless the respondent had a different standard in mind, like reliably implementing unfamiliar algorithms rather than reproducing a familiar example such as quicksort.

People may not know exactly what current systems can do, and they may interpret the same question differently. So I’d treat the surveys as evidence about what researchers believe, rather than as a definitive assessment of capabilities or when they’ll arrive. It’s useful to look at the individual questions and ask whether we’re actually measuring the thing we intended to measure.

r001.rationale: It mentions reliably implementing unfamiliar algorithms, but does not say the milestone is for algorithms absent from the model’s training data.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish an aggregate of respondents’ probabilities from the percentage of respondents predicting the milestone.

r003.rationale: It says a familiar quicksort example may not establish reliable implementation of unfamiliar algorithms.

r004.rationale: It does not identify that the survey question leaves the required frequency of success unspecified.

r005.rationale: It does not suggest that asking about a capability may lead respondents to infer AI cannot yet perform it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the explanation is that those forecasts were made before people had seen systems like ChatGPT. So if it can now do the task as specified, that’s evidence that the forecasts were too conservative on that question.

But I’d also want to look carefully at the wording. There can be a difference between producing an implementation of quicksort, which is something you can find many examples of, and reliably implementing an unfamiliar algorithm from a description. Seeing one successful example doesn’t necessarily establish the broader capability the respondents had in mind.

That said, I wouldn’t want to explain away every surprising result by saying the question must have meant something harder. If the system meets the stated criterion, we should count that and update our expectations. These surveys are measurements of what people expect, not guarantees that those expectations are well calibrated.

r001.rationale: It contrasts familiar examples with unfamiliar algorithms, but does not say the milestone is meant to cover algorithms absent from the model’s training data.

r002.rationale: It describes surveys as measurements of expectations but does not distinguish aggregate probabilities from the share of respondents predicting the milestone.

r003.rationale: It says one successful quicksort example does not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar algorithm-implementation tasks.

r004.rationale: It does not identify that the survey leaves the required success frequency unspecified.

r005.rationale: It does not suggest that listing a capability on the survey could lead respondents to infer that AI cannot yet perform it.
